newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa denies Biko's interrogators found. [CORRECTED 20:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: S.Africa denies Biko's interrogators found. [CORRECTED 20:00 GMT]

text.p: (Corrects to change headline to "S.Africa denies Biko's interrogators found" and replaces all references to "killers" with "interrogators" throughout).

South Africa's Truth Commission denied on Monday that the policemen who had interrogated 1970s black leader Steve Biko had come forward and sought pardon, but said preliminary inquiries about amnesty had been made.

Phila Ngqumba, spokesman in the Eastern Cape region for Archbishop Desmond Tutu's statutory Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC), said the riddle of Biko's death in police custody in September 1977 had not been solved.

Responding to a newspaper report that named five former policemen as Biko's interrogators and which said they had decided to seek amnesty, Ngqumba said: "We have not received any amnesty application concerning Biko's death.
"There are lawyers making inquiries, but as far as I am concerned that is as far as it has gone," Ngqumba said.

Biko, who died of brain damage in a Pretoria prison cell, was the most prominent black activist to die while detained without trial under draconian security laws used to suppress opposition to apartheid.

People who knew him as the charismatic leader of the Black Consciousness Movement say he would have been the only person who could have challenged Nelson Mandela for election as South Africa's first black president.

Mandela's African National Congress said in a statement opponents of apartheid had never doubted that Biko, whose death was dramatised in the Richard Attenborough film "Cry Freedom", was killed by government agents.
The party urged torturers and doctors implicated in the abuse of apartheid foes to "break ranks with the past and expose the real masterminds behind these deeds".
The Eastern Province Herald in Port Elizabeth on Monday named five former security policeman as Biko's interrogators and said they intended to seek pardon from the TRC.
The commission has until the end of the year to unravel the human rights record of apartheid and the war against it and is authorised to pardon offenders and to compensate victims.
The TRC scheduled a news conference in Port Elizabeth on Tuesday, but Ngqumba said it concerned other alleged police assassinations in the area and not the Biko case.
Biko was detained without charge in Port Elizabeth in August 1977. He was later driven naked and chained in the back of a police van to Pretoria, where his interrogation continued.
He died in prison less than a week after he left Port Elizabeth. Though his body showed evidence of sustained torture, an inquest failed to identify anyone responsible for his death.
At least eight prominent anti-apartheid leaders disappeared or were assassinated in the Eastern Cape province, which is also Mandela's home, during the last two decades of white rule.

Confessions about these killings could lead Tutu's commission to those who controlled state death squads alleged also to have been responsible for scores of less publicised killings, including the massacre of train passengers.
